lines.text: The generator handed you a robot that drives, on a file full of guesses. Now you replace them with measured numbers, starting with the motors that aim the wheels.
Steering is a position loop with nothing pulling it down, so the gravity gain drops out. You're adjusting the generator's numbers, not starting from zero.
Flick the stick and watch the measured angle chase the commanded one. If it lags, shoots past or buzzes, change one number, redeploy, and flick again.
Wheel radius is the one you can probably skip. Only measure it if you've changed wheels, or the robot's idea of distance disagrees with a tape measure.
Here the robot went less far than it reported, so the radius in the file was too big, and it comes down.
Top speed has a trap. Full stick asks for exactly the number in the file, so a plateau sitting right on it tells you nothing about the robot. Raise it until the robot falls short.
Slip current needs a wall and one drive motor, with the voltage ramped up slowly.
Watch for the instant velocity jumps and current drops. That's the tire letting go, and you want the peak just before it.
Keep each ramp short. A motor pushing a wall it can't move is stalled, and it heats up fast.
The drive gains only matter because every drive request in this course asks for a wheel speed. The generator's version sends the stick straight to volts and never reads them.
On a speed loop, feedforward does nearly all of the work, so it's tuned first. Keep the wheels on the ground, because a wheel in the air has no load.
The deadband keeps a worn stick from creeping the robot across the field. Halve it until the wheel targets twitch with your hands off, then go back one.
Drive a square, and check that the robot comes back to its tape with the pose near zero. Autonomous leans on that pose next, with nobody on the sticks.
